messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Eleanor was seventy-eight when the Marshall Fire tore through her Colorado neighborhood, devouring everything in its path. She and her husband Robert had twenty minutes to grab their go-bag and their elderly cat, but the cat panicked and ran under the bed; by the time Eleanor coaxed her out, the smoke was so thick she couldn't see. They made it to the car, but Eleanor’s childhood friend Margaret, who lived two doors down, turned back for her dog and never came out. The fire was later ruled an accident—a downed power line—and the utility company paid a fine but admitted no fault. The official report used words like “unprecedented” and “act of God,” and Eleanor felt the bottom drop out of her understanding of fairness.

In the months afterward, Eleanor tried to return to her freelance graphic design work from a temporary apartment, but the world felt unrecognizable. She had always believed that if you worked hard and were good to people, life would be fair; that belief was gone now, replaced by a quiet certainty that the world was actively dangerous and that what happened to her was deeply unjust and no one had done anything about it. This conviction seeped into everything. When a door slammed in the apartment hallway, her heart seized—the sound seemed to confirm that danger could come from anywhere, at any moment, without warning. The same happened when she caught a whiff of alcohol; a neighbor’s beer at a barbecue made her stomach knot because she smelled it on the man who had refused to evacuate, laughing and drinking on his porch while the fire crested the ridge. And when a friend at the senior center talked about her son’s recent loss of a spouse, Eleanor had to excuse herself—she couldn’t bear to hear the words “lost” or “gone,” because they yanked her back into the belief that the world was not just dangerous but pointlessly cruel.

She began cleaning. Every morning, she scrubbed the kitchen counters until they gleamed; she reorganized the pantry by height and then by color; she dusted the same shelf three times in an hour. The compulsive organizing gave her a fragile sense of control, a small rebellion against the chaos that had swallowed her life. She also caught herself dwelling, endlessly looped, on how the fire could have been prevented: if the power company had trimmed the trees, if the evacuation order had come earlier, if she had grabbed the cat sooner. The rumination felt like a kind of mental labor, as though she could undo the event by sheer force of thought. And when the images became unbearable, she tried to erase the memory entirely—she would put on loud music, scrub a spot on the floor, will herself to stop seeing Margaret’s face at the door.

But the memory fought back. Sometimes Eleanor could narrate the event in a flat, detached voice, as if it happened to a stranger, and that numbness frightened her more than the panic. At other moments, the memory roared in and felt as present as the room around her—she would be slicing vegetables and suddenly be back in the smoky driveway, the heat on her skin, the cat yowling. The extreme nature of it all made the story feel almost unreal, as though it couldn’t have happened to her, even as the flashback pinned her in place. She tried harder to push it away, but the more she cleaned and ruminated, the more the memory intruded. The cleaning became a trigger itself: each time she dusted a picture frame, she saw the room that once held it, and the door-slam of a cabinet would send her spiraling into the belief that she was never safe. She felt trapped in a cycle where her own strategies to cope only sharpened the very triggers and memories she was trying to escape.

Three years later, Eleanor still works as a graphic designer, but she has stopped taking jobs that involve meeting clients in their homes—the unfamiliar doors, the sudden slams. She works exclusively from her new house, which she has arranged in rigid order, and she avoids the news about natural disasters entirely. Last week, her husband gently asked if she wanted to attend a memorial for Margaret. The question sent her into a three-day cleaning binge that left her hands raw. She finally called a therapist because she was terrified that she would never feel safe again, and because, despite all her efforts, the memory of the fire still felt more real than anything in her current life.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not contain a causal link where negative appraisals (e.g., beliefs that the world is dangerous or unjust) lead to the intrusion of the traumatic memory; instead, memory intrudes independently or is triggered by external cues.

The vignette shows triggers leading to negative appraisals, but not the reverse: negative appraisals causing or creating new triggers; it does not convey that the appraisal itself generates the triggers.
